en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-puṣpasaṃcaya-dhāraṇī-mantra-sūtra*.
Translator unknown; now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the palace of the Naga King Anavatapta, together with...
There were five hundred bhikṣus together with them,
and one thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
all of whom were in their final birth before buddhahood.
They all attain the stage of dhāraṇī and rank among those on the ten bhūmis;
just as a prince will before long succeed to the royal throne,
so too it is with these bodhisattvas.
Adorned with great merit, they shall before long attain the rank of consecration and achieve Buddhahood.
These bodhisattvas have each come from the Buddha-worlds of other directions to assemble here.
Regarding all Buddhas, his mind was free from doubt or obstruction.
At that time, within the assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Siṃhavikrāmin.
Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground,
joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One, if there be sons or daughters of good family..."
"If one were to provide all manner of requisites for enjoyment to the Tathāgata for the remainder of their entire life,
would they gain much merit?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin:
Do not speak thus or give rise to doubt;
making offerings to the Tathāgata yields immense merit. Why is this?

The Tathāgata possesses immeasurable virtue of precepts, immeasurable dhyāna-concentration and samādhi, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable liberation, and immeasurable knowledge and vision of liberation;
this is likewise true for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas.
Furthermore, the merit of all worthy ones and sages is exceedingly great and immeasurable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken, gave rise to faith and understanding in his heart.
They redoubled their reverence, making offerings, honoring, and praising him;
they provided him with robes, dwellings, bedding, and medicinal decoctions for illness,
as well as all such various articles of comfort.
They shall all provide offerings so that nothing is lacking.
If there are good men or good women who,
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata...
If one takes even as much of the Buddha’s relics as a single mustard seed to offer worship and prostrations,
the merit of this is exactly equal to the previous merit.
Furthermore, if another person were to take the seven precious jewels in quantities as vast as Mount Sumeru...
“If one were to practice giving to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas throughout a single kalpa,
would the merit obtained be great?
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said: "If there are those, whether monastics or laypeople,
who can take even a single coin to give as a gift to one who has first resolved to attain bodhicitta,
the merit they obtain shall be compared to the previous merit [of the former case]."
A hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-millionth part does not equal even one;
indeed, it cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.
It is exactly so, just as the Buddha has taught.
Furthermore, if there should be a person who,
while traveling on a desolate road after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
sees a stūpa or temple of the Tathāgata.
If any son or daughter of good family can offer even a single flower, a single lamp or candle,
or a lump of clay used as an offering before an image;
If there are good men or good women who offer even a single copper coin to an image of the Buddha for the purpose of its repair and maintenance.
If one uses a handful of water to sprinkle upon the ground of a Buddha-stūpa to remove impurities,
withered flowers, and candle remains;
or if one offers incense as an offering.
If one takes even a single step toward a stupa or temple,
or utters "Namo Buddha" just once,
it would be impossible to cause such a person to fall into the three evil realms.
"Even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, such a thing could never occur.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita,
"There is a dhāraṇī called 'Flower Cluster' (Puṣpasaṃcaya)."
It brings great benefit to the devas and people of the world.
Those who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and practice it according to the Dharma will obtain merit many times greater than that mentioned above.
Furthermore, there may be good sons who make offerings to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; yet these offerings,
even by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, do not equal one-tenth of that [former offering].
To such an extent that it cannot be known even through calculation or analogy.
When such a person’s life ends, they will never be born in one of the eight difficult states or into a lowly family.
In whatever place they are born, their six sense faculties will be complete.
They naturally remember their past lives,
constantly encounter the Triple Gem, behold the Buddhas,
and hear the Dharma; they never forget the mind of bodhi.
They will be able to attain profound and immeasurable eloquence;
riding upon the six supernormal powers, they will travel to the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions to receive the sublime Dharma and transform sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke the mantra, saying:

Tadita | Dharani | Dharaṇi | Dharaṇi | Madibha | Bubhasani | Sitī | Cāntī | Nirmuci | Nirhārī | Lūgapati | Buddhapati | Tiri | Ukaraji-karaji | Rājupagati | Tejovati | Viśrabhoti | Dharmaprasī | Acchaya-kepi-kapphavati | Amita-kepi | Hutasani | Tejovati | Nikubhamakhivati | Tejogahavati | Indriya-bhoti | Dhitabuddhe | Svāhā. The Buddha said: "There may be sons of good family or daughters of good family."
Those who wish to practice this dhāraṇī should do so during the second or third month, or within the eight months [of the year],
from the eighth day to the fifteenth day of the waxing moon.
Having purified oneself by bathing and donned new, clean garments,
one should sit before an image of the Buddha in a quiet place,
hanging silk streamers, banners, and canopies.
Make offerings of incense and flowers, prostrate, and perform repentance.
Recite this dhāraṇī during the six periods of the day and night;
whether sitting or walking, do not allow the mind to become distracted.
When seven days have passed, you shall behold the Buddha.
If you do not see him, continue to recite this dhāraṇī with single-minded devotion for another two weeks, three weeks, or seven days.
One will certainly see the Buddha seated upon a lotus flower preaching the Dharma.
At that time, one immediately attains the power of self-recollection of past lives (*jātismara*), and one’s power of mindfulness becomes firm.
One obtains *dhāraṇī* and unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*), whether seeking extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) or seeking meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Whether seeking wisdom or eloquence;
whether seeking medical arts or incantations;
whether seeking craftsmanship or literary arts.
In this way, all various aspirations of the mind shall be fully realized;
they will never be forgotten until the attainment of Buddhahood,
with the exception of the Four Noble Truths.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin,
the devas, humans, asuras, and the assembly of bhikṣus,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sutra on the Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Flower Cluster Spoken by the Buddha.
